THROW-FORWARD: On the Run

By: Laura Byrne | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A glimpse into a world of treacherous waters, rival teams and the promise of a bounty!

Unique Selling Point:
Unrivalled access to the sardine run, with underwater footage, drones, intense characters and action.

Summary:
Every winter, the sardine run hits the KwaZulu Natal Coast… And the hunt begins. Rival crews take to the deadly waters hoping for the ultimate catch. We preview an upcoming episode of Carte Blanche: the triumphs, the tragedies, and the crews who risk it all or lose it all. This is On the Run.

Script:


(Macfarlane) Pretoria: South Africa's administrative capital. Statues… bureaucracy… old power. But this is also Pitori: a living rebellion. Townships that take pride in a language born of the dark history of this country.



(Macfarlane) It's called Sepitori, and it thrives in Pretoria's townships.



(Macfarlane) One of them is Soshanguve: it's very name an acronym of Sotho, Shangaan, Nguni, and Venda. People who were forced together, and in response, created a rich tapestry of language.

 

(Macfarlane) Each of Pretoria's townships has its own iconic features. Soshanguve boasts what might be the highest concentration of South Africa's legendary Toyota Ventures in one area. But they all share a common linguistic thread.

 

(Macfarlane) They call this place ‘Pitori Mahlanyeng’ – the ‘place of crazy people’. But don’t let that madness fool you. It’s the kind of madness that births revolutions.



(Presley Chweneyagae Subtitles) Hey, sonny. What did I tell you? What did I say?



(Boy Subtitles) - Don’t start with me.



(Presley Chweneyagae Subtitles) - Of course I’ll start with you. I told you leave

My sister’s job alone, right? Huh?



(Boy Subtitles) But I need that job.



(Presley Chweneyagae Subtitles) Don’t talk rubbish. Do you think this is Pietersburg?



(Macfarlane) Before The River, hearing SePitori on prime-time TV was like expecting pap and vleis at a high tea. It was confined to the townships - not featured on what was deemed proper television. But executive producer Phathu Makwarela made a radical choice. He set his television drama against the backdrop of Gauteng’s mining industry - not in Joburg, but in a Pretoria informal settlement.



(Phathu Makwarela) In hindsight now, you think, oh, that was a risky move. What if it had gone to an end where nobody could get this language, nobody could get these characters?



(Macfarlane) Especially because those characters speak raw SePitori - led by the late Presley Chueneyagae.

 

(Macfarlane) Although he was born in far-away, Setswana-speaking Mahikeng, in playing the charismatic villain, Cobra, Chueneyagae mastered Sepitori’s rhythm and soul.



(Presley Chweneyagae Subtitles) I told you guys I’d live the good life. Hey?



(Macfarlane) Watching Presley as Cobra, you weren’t hearing scripted dialogue. You were hearing Pitori’s heartbeat – raw, real, and finally on show.



(Presley Chweneyagae Subtitles) Hey, I’m talking to you, man!



(Phathu Makwarela) What was interesting was that he wasn't the first option. So, we had looked at a lot of actors for the role, because we were still looking for that SePitori tone. Because when you meet him, he is very pure Tswana. And then you say action, and then he transformed. I think internally I was jumping up and down with joy. Cause I was like, yes!



(Macfarlane) This is what I wanted.



(Phathu) This is what I want.



(Macfarlane) Subtitling a language like SePitori presents a unique challenge.



(Macfarlane Subtitles) When someone says, “My brother, you’re killing it.”



(Macfarlane) How do you even explain in subtitles?



(Phathu Makwarela) I think what you lose in subtitles, most of the time, it's always the nuance.



(MacFaralane) The nuance and context.



(Phathu Makwarela) I think you kind of miss, like 40% of the juice that makes the language even richer and beautiful.



(Macfarlane) But the cast's passion helped convey meaning - even in an unfamiliar language.



(Nokuthula Ledwaba) I hang out in the township, quite a lot for research, to see friends, to see family. So, it was pretty easy to talk to either Pathu or the creative producer at the time, that listen, this doesn't quite work in this particular story that we're telling. Can we rather opt to do this? This is the objective. So that helped a lot when it came to maintaining the realness, the rawness of the story itself.



(Macfarlane) Remember Soshanguve? That's the hometown of actress Nokuthula Ledwaba, known to The River fans as Cobra's on-and-off girlfriend Angelina. She says bringing SePitori to the screen satisfied a craving audience didn't know they had.



(Nokuthula Ledwaba) Look, there was a hunger. The hunger had been there for a long, long time, from the audience itself, even for me as an actor. There needs to be something that reminds us of the forgotten people. When the River came, and everyone was like… there it is. People were like we are seen, we are heard, we are here. Cause we have always had our own music, we had our own everything.



(MacFaralne) Yes.



(Nokuthula Ledwaba) We had a culture that was uniquely ours.



(MacFarlane) So, you can’t come to Pitori without enjoying this meal. Everywhere else around the country, it’s called Kota, Skhambane, Bunny Chow, but in Pitori, it’s “Sphatlho”.



(Macfarlane) Hmm, Bra!



(Prof. Ditsele) One example that I use is the word Sphatlho. I know, in southern parts of Gauteng, they call it Kota.



(Macfarlane) Kota or skhambane, depending where you come from.



(Prof. Ditsele) Yes, here they call it sphatlo. We don’t have a standard word for sphatiho in Setswana, right? So why not use it?



(Macfarlane) Tshwane University of Technology’s Professor Thabo Ditsele is a linguist who has researched Sepitori for years. He insists that it should be recognised as more than township slang - and says it predates apartheid’s forced removals.



(Prof. Thabo Ditsele) I’ve argued that it’s a language. It’s not a variety of some other language, right? So, townships, like, I mean, Marabastad, before the Group Areas Act, People spoke SePitori then.



(Macfarlane) In 1950, the Group Areas Act was passed, forcing people into areas designated by race - a permanent displacement.



(Prof. Thabo Ditsele) They travelled with SePitori. So, it’s always been around. So, you could argue that the current townships, as we know them, are younger than SePitori.



(Macfarlane) Here’s Ditsele’s big argument: Sepitori’s raw street-smart energy? Don’t dismiss it – use it to power up South Africa’s other languages.



(Prof Thabo Ditsele) So it’s good that varieties like SePitori would emerge. By emerging, they keep up with the times, they are flourishing us with terms that we need to embrace and grow our languages. So, if you want an African language in South Africa to grow, allow varieties like SePitori to exist, to feed it with terminologies.



(Macfarlane) Mamelodi, the very name means mother of melodies, and she lives up to it. From struggle songs to iconic Kwaito songs that are claiming our streets, everyone knows,



(Macfarlane Subtitles) Pretoria is indeed a place of madness.



(Macfarlane) One of Pretoria’s most acclaimed voices is Amapiano star, Focalistic. He brandishes Sepitori like a badge of honour, putting it front and centre in his music.



(Focalistic) It's a community, right? And just like other communities, you kind of get left out in terms of, like, institutionalisation, or 1 2 3, but representation is there, you know, the songs are there. I always say, like, you know, we did over 100 million streams. All in all, like in my career, when I look at just Apple Music, over 100 million streams cannot just be people from Pretoria, do you understand.



(Focalistic Subtitles) So, it's on a level that’s quite high.



(Macfarlane) Are we doing enough to express ourselves? You know, because everybody wants to sound American, everybody wants to sound European, everybody wants to sound anything else, but where they come from?



(Focalistic) Oh, are we doing enough? Is a crazy question. I don't think so, and I don't think we will ever do enough. But the best way to explain this thing, if it's a problem that we need to solve, is institutionalisation, you know, like having an official Hall of Fame is, you know, a big step in the right direction, you know,



(Focalistic Subtitles) And we did that, on other subjects...



(Focalistic) You can go to a planetarium. You can go to you know ...



(Focalistic Subtitles) But there’s a little about where to go, you know, to learn music and culture.



(Focalistic) And that’s the heartbeat of the youth. You know, if you want to say anything to influence the youth, put it in a song.



(Macfarlane) What’s crazy is how a one (I can’t hear the word) township lingo SePitori has now become the heartbeat of Amapiano and prime-time TV.



(Macfarlane) Presley gave SePitori its swagger. Focalistic gave it beats. It’s a model for a nation wrestling with its own identity.



(Macfarlane) A language that’s unapologetic, evolving, and alive.
